# Charts as FLines

A `Chart` is a plot made of FLines. Use it when the plot has to sit in the same drawing as your other FLines, when you want to click on its marks, or when you want to draw an expected range and see which data falls outside it. For everything else, Plotly is better.

You build a `Chart` up a call at a time and hand it to `showChart`. `showChart(c)`,
`display(channel, c)`, `c.h`, and a box whose last expression is a `Chart` all render the same
figure. Here is a residual curve with an expected bound:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
Chart(title = "residual per iteration", xLabel = "iteration", yLabel = "|r|")
    .line("residual", iterations, residual)
    .points("residual", iterations, residual)
    .expect(max = 1e-6, because = "converged below 1e-6")
```

## Reach for Plotly first

Field already has Plotly: `linePlot`, `scatter`, `violin`, `showSignals`, each described in the
reference under [`plotly.kt`](reference/visualization.md#plotly-kt). The shortest of them puts named
signals on screen in one call:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
showSignals("residual" to residual, "step" to step, title = "per iteration")
```

The others return a `Plot` for you to `display`; [DoughDSP: hear the primitives](dough_dsp_sound.md)
uses `showSignals` throughout. Plotly has real text, a legend with line swatches, axes that
autorange, and it reflows to whatever shape you give it. A `Chart` is fixed geometry fitted and
centred in its panel, so a panel of a different shape leaves empty margin, and its text scales with
the figure.

Use a `Chart` instead when you need one of these:

- the plot drawn under the same transform as other FLine geometry, which Plotly cannot join;
- clicking a mark and getting back the datum it stands for;
- `expect()`, which draws an expected range on the plot.

## The marks

`points`, `line`, `area`, `bars`, `histogram`, plus `rule`, `vrule` and `band` for annotation. Marks
over the same numbers share one frame and one legend.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val xs = (0..120).map { it / 120.0 * 6.28318 }
val decay = xs.map { exp(-it * 0.25) * sin(it * 2.0) }
val envelope = xs.map { exp(-it * 0.25) }

Chart(title = "line, area and points share one frame", xLabel = "t (radians)", yLabel = "amplitude")
    .area("envelope", xs, envelope)
    .line("damped sine", xs, decay)
    .points("samples", xs.filterIndexed { i, _ -> i % 8 == 0 },
                       decay.filterIndexed { i, _ -> i % 8 == 0 })
```

![Three marks in one frame: a filled envelope area, a damped sine line through it, and every eighth sample as a green dot](assets/chart_gallery/chart-marks-lines-and-points.png)

`bars` takes categories and puts them on the axis, so you do not index them yourself:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
Chart(title = "bars put their categories on the axis", yLabel = "gates")
    .bars("cost", ["xor", "maj3", "adder", "mux", "parity"], [6, 11, 27, 4, 19])
```

![Five bars labelled xor, maj3, adder, mux and parity, with their categories written under them on the axis](assets/chart_gallery/chart-bars-categorical.png)

`histogram` bins for you by Sturges' rule:

![A histogram of 600 samples from two overlapping Gaussians, twelve bins wide, counts on the y axis](assets/chart_gallery/chart-histogram-sturges.png)

## Scales and ticks

`Scale(lo, hi, pixelLo, pixelHi, kind)` maps data to pixels with `toPixel`/`toData`. A y scale is
built inverted, because y grows downwards in Field's 2D outputs.

The tick functions are public, so you can use them for an axis of your own: `niceTicks(lo, hi, target)`, `logTicks`, `niceNumber`, `tickLabel` and
`tickLabels`.

Values are snapped to their own step, so an axis never reads `0.30000000000000004`, and `tickLabels`
picks one notation for a whole axis rather than per label.

Set `xKind`/`yKind` to `ScaleKind.LOG` for a log axis. A log scale refuses a non-positive domain,
and a non-positive datum is left out of the plot.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val n = (1..6).map { 10.0.pow(it) }
val time = n.map { it * 1.4e-6 + 3e-4 }

Chart(title = "a log axis, and decade ticks", xLabel = "n", yLabel = "seconds")
    .also { it.xKind = ScaleKind.LOG; it.yKind = ScaleKind.LOG }
    .line("measured", n, time)
    .points("measured", n, time)
```

![A log-log plot over six decades, ticks at 1.0e+01 through 1.0e+06 on x and 0.001 through 1 on y](assets/chart_gallery/chart-log-scale-decades.png)

## `expect()`: drawing what the data should do

`expect(min, max, series, because)` draws the expectation: the accepted range becomes a band across the
plot, the bounds it names are ruled, data outside recolours, and the footnote counts the violations.
An unbounded side draws no edge, which is the visual difference between "at most 1e-6" and "between
0 and 1e-6".

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
Chart(title = "residual per iteration", xLabel = "iteration", yLabel = "|r|", note = "Adam, lr 0.05")
    .line("residual", iterations, residual)
    .points("residual", iterations, residual)
    .expect(max = 1e-6, because = "converged below 1e-6")
```

![A residual curve that converges but spikes twice above the expectation band; the bound is ruled at 1e-6, four points are red, and the footnote reads 4 points outside expectation](assets/chart_gallery/chart-expect-a-claim-you-can-watch-fail.png)

- `Chart.deviations` returns the points outside the expectation, so a test can assert on the same
  list the footnote counts. There is also a predicate form,
  `expect(series, because) { x, y -> … }`, with no shape to draw.
- Each datum is counted once. A `line` for the trend plus `points` to make it clickable is two
  marks over one datum, and the footnote counts that datum once.

## Marks pick themselves up

`Box.lines` switches to the interactive SVG renderer the moment any line carries `onClick` or
`hoverColor`. Point and bar marks set both, plus a `label` naming the datum, so you can hover over a bar
or click a point with no extra setup:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val c = Chart(yLabel = "gates").bars("cost", "xor" to 6, "adder" to 27)
c.onPick = { pick -> print("${pick.series}/${pick.category} = ${pick.y}") }
showChart(c)
```

Set `pickable = false` to turn this off. A series with more data than `pickLimit` (400 by
default) stops responding point by point.

## From a DataFrame

`DataFrame<*>.chart()` picks the axes so you do not have to name them for a quick look: the first
numeric column for x if the frame has two or more, otherwise the first column as categories,
otherwise the row index; then every remaining numeric column as a series.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val people = dataFrameOf("name", "age")("Alice", 15, "Bob", 30, "Cara", 45)

people.chart()             // bars: age per name
people.chart(x = "age")    // age on the x axis
showChart(runs)            // straight from a frame to the screen
```

Series are capped for auto-selection, because a legend stops being readable past a handful of
entries, and the per-datum dots are dropped automatically for a frame with more rows than `pickLimit`. See
[DataFrames in a Box](dataframe.md).

## Keeping a figure inside its frame

The panel a `Chart` lands in is fitted to the geometry it actually draws, so anything drawn outside
`width` × `height` would make the whole figure smaller. `clip`, on by default, prevents that in two
ways:

- mark geometry is cut to `plotRect`: lines and area outlines by Liang–Barsky, an area's fill
  by Sutherland–Hodgman so it stays closed, a point outside dropped whole, a bar clamped on both
  axes and dropped when no part of it is in the window, a rule or a band that falls off the axis not
  drawn at all. A clipped series stays *one* `FLine` with several subpaths, so it is still one
  series, one legend entry, and one thing to hover;
- `title` and `note` are wrapped to the figure width, capped at two and four
  lines with an ellipsis past that.

Clipping only matters when you set an explicit `xDomain` or `yDomain`, because a derived domain
always covers its own data.

Set `clip = false` when you are composing a chart with other
FLine geometry under a shared transform and want the overflow.

## Down to geometry

`toFLines()` lowers the whole figure to `List<FLine>` in pixel space and `plotRect()` reports the
rectangle the marks are clipped to, so the chart can go
into the same drawing as the rest of your geometry, under one transform. `toHTML()` goes through
`afield.ui.visualization.linesToHTML`, the same markup `Box.lines` builds.

Labels are glyph outlines. On a machine with no fonts, the chart is drawn without labels.

Text of your own goes in as `TextLayout.toFLines()` (one line per glyph) or `toFLine()` (one for
the whole string). Move it with `FLine.transform`, which carries each curve's control points with its
end points.

# Geometry from disk You have a mesh file, and you want to see it in Field and then compute with it. For every format, that is one line: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} showMesh("/path/to/thing.glb") ``` That reads the file, assembles it, and puts a shaded render you can orbit into the box's output area, with the mesh's measurements printed underneath. Keep the mesh instead of the picture and everything in the [mesh family](mesh_examples.md) applies: weld it, measure its volume, decimate it, shoot a ray at it, write it back out as something else. ## What reads what
| you have | the call | what you get back | works headless | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `.obj` | `meshFromFile(path)` | `TriMesh`, index-for-index with the file | yes | | `.stl` (ASCII or binary) | `meshFromFile(path)` | `TriMesh`, triangle soup — see [below](#what-each-format-loses) | yes | | `.ply` (ASCII, binary, either endianness) | `meshFromAnyFile(path)` | `TriMesh` with the file's per-vertex colours | yes | | `.glb`, `.gltf`, `.fbx`, `.dae`, `.3ds`, … | `meshFromAnyFile(path)` | `TriMesh`, all parts baked through their node transforms | yes | | any of the above, textured, with PBR materials | `gltfModelHere("…")` / the [Fabricate renderer](fabricate_renderer.md) | GPU buffers, materials, textures, a live scene | no — needs a renderer | | `.step`, `.iges`, `.brep` | **nothing** | — | — |
`meshFromAnyFile` handles everything `meshFromFile` does and more, so if you are unsure, use it. `meshFromFile` is the pure-Kotlin reader with no native library behind it. Where each loader lives in the source is at the [end of the page](#internals-where-the-loaders-live). Two renderers put a mesh on screen, and both take a `TriMesh`. `showMesh` sends it to the Three.js viewer, where you can orbit it; it is the same viewer `threeLines(...)` draws FLines in, so a solid and its annotations can share one scene. Pass `renderer = MeshRenderer.CPU` for a still image drawn on the CPU instead, which needs no GPU; `TriMesh.renderPng` and the inline `toHTML()` card use the same renderer. ## A real GLB, in a real output area This example loads the Khronos ToyCar sample, the same GLB the [Fabricate renderer](fabricate_renderer.md) renders with full PBR materials. It has three mesh/material buckets, a draped cloth with a lot of folds, glass, and every part positioned by a node transform rather than baked into the vertices: ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/geometry_from_disk/toycar.png" wait="14.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" padding="20"} :::static // The same file public/docs/fabricate_renderer.md renders with full PBR — here through the plain // Three.js viewer instead, which is `showMesh`'s default and gives you a solid you can orbit. // `renderer = MeshRenderer.CPU` for the static z-buffer figure, which needs no GPU at all. val glb = java.io.File("public/docs/assets/fabricate_demo/ToyCar.glb") println("${glb.name}: ${glb.length()} bytes on disk") val car = meshFromAnyFile(glb.path) println(car.summary()) // Three mesh/material buckets, assembled by node transform rather than heaped at the origin. val b = car.bounds() println("assembled extent %.4f x %.4f x %.4f metres".format( b.max.x - b.min.x, b.max.y - b.min.y, b.max.z - b.min.z)) :::fold draw it showMesh( car, view = MeshView(width = 560, height = 420, wireframe = false), title = "ToyCar.glb — 108,936 triangles in the Three.js viewer", ) :::endfold ``` ![The Khronos ToyCar GLB in Field's Three.js viewer: a 1950s saloon model sitting on a heavily draped cloth, correctly shaded with soft folds, above a caption reading 77429 verts, 108936 tris, extent 0.073 x 0.029 x 0.074, chi=1909, open](assets/geometry_from_disk/toycar.png) The caption under the picture is the mesh's own measurements: - **77,429 vertices, 108,936 triangles** (326,808 indices), summed over the three buckets: ToyCar itself at 66,951 vertices, Fabric at 8,959 and Glass at 1,519. - **extent 0.073 × 0.029 × 0.074** — the file is in metres, and it is a 7 cm toy. `MeshView`'s `distance` is measured in bounding-sphere radii, so the camera frames it correctly without your having to know that. `normalized(2.0)` is there if you want a common scale across several models. - **χ = 1909, open, 2782 boundary loops.** χ is the Euler characteristic. An artist's model is a shell rather than a solid, and every UV seam and every hard edge is a real cut in the surface. Expect this of anything that came out of a modeller, and do not reach for `repaired()` unless you actually need watertightness (for a volume, a boolean, or a printer). !!! warning "Loading a glTF without a renderer" `GltfSupport.loadGltfBasic(path)` with **default arguments cannot run outside a live renderer**. `GltfLoadConfig.loadTextures` defaults to `true`, and that path asks the box context for a `Renderer` so it can build stub textures. From a plain function, a test, or a headless script it therefore dies with a bare `NullPointerException` that says nothing about textures. Pass `GltfLoadConfig(loadTextures = false)` and geometry-only loading works everywhere. `assimpToTriMesh` does exactly that for you. ## What happens to a glTF scene A glTF file is a node hierarchy: each node carries a **full 4×4 transform**, several nodes can reference the same mesh, and each mesh carries its own material. Flattening that into one `TriMesh` keeps some of it and drops the rest. The table says what `meshFromAnyFile` does with each part, checked on a small scene of one asymmetric triangle instanced by an identity node, a translated node, a *child* of that translated node, and a **mirrored** node with `scale (-1, 1, 1)`.
| the scene has | the bridge does | |---|---| | several nodes referencing meshes | **merges all of them.** Four instances arrive as 4 triangles in 4 components, not "the first one". | | a node transform | **applies it.** ToyCar's own three nodes each carry a uniform `1e-4` scale, so a bridge that dropped transforms would render the figure above 10,000× too big: 730 m across, not 0.073 m. | | a parent chain | **composes it.** The child of the node translated by `(3, 0, 0)`, itself translated by `(0, 2, 0)`, lands at `(3, 2, 0)`. | | a **mirror** — negative determinant | applies it, **and reverses that part's winding**, so the surface still faces outward instead of being culled away. | | non-uniform scale | normals go through the **inverse transpose**, not the matrix, so they stay perpendicular to the surface. | | per-vertex `COLOR_0` | kept, per instance. An all-white array — what glTF writes when the file has no colours — is dropped. | | quads or n-gons | already triangles: Assimp's `aiProcess_Triangulate` runs before the bridge sees anything. | | materials and textures | **dropped.** A `TriMesh` has no concept of a texture. Use the [Fabricate renderer](fabricate_renderer.md) for those. | | animation | **dropped.** The bind pose is baked; node TRS tracks and skinning are not read. | | a Y-up / Z-up disagreement | **nothing.** glTF is Y-up by specification and no axis conversion is applied, so a Z-up PLY or OBJ arrives on its side. `rotated(...)` is yours to apply. |

A mirrored node arrives with 3×3 determinant −1.0 and `bindPose.toMatrix()` gives it back at +1.0: the reflection is gone, the instance is placed un-mirrored, and nothing warns you. `bindMatrix` is the un-decomposed world matrix, and it is what `assimpToTriMesh` and the GPU paths read. `FabricateTransform` is itself a TRS triple, so `FabricateTransform.set(Matrix4f)` checks its own decomposition and keeps the original matrix when recomposing does not reproduce it. A `heightfieldMesh` round-trips its uvs to within 1e-5. The coordinates always survive: area and volume are identical to six decimal places through every route, so a mesh whose *shape* changed on a round trip is a bug and not a format. OBJ keeps structure and loses colour. It indexes positions, normals and uvs separately, so Field's reader emits one vertex per distinct `(position, uv, normal)` corner — which is why a hard-edged cube from a modeller faithfully comes back with 24 vertices and not 8. There is no standardised per-vertex colour in OBJ, so `withColor` never reaches the file. STL keeps nothing but triangles: no vertex sharing at all, so 1280 triangles become 3840 unshared vertices and every edge reads as a boundary. `weld(1e-5)` recovers the topology exactly but not the normals, because STL never stored one per vertex, so re-shade after welding — `shadedNormals(35.0)` is usually right. PLY is the format that carries colour, which is generally why a file is a PLY at all: it is what photogrammetry and scanners emit, and `meshFromAnyFile` routes `.ply` through `PlySupport` rather than Assimp for that reason. File size for the same 1280 triangles, with binary STL's exactly `84 + 50n` bytes as the floor: | Format | bytes | |---|---| | binary `.stl` | 64,084 | | `.obj` | 75,625 | | ASCII `.stl` | 324,825 | ## Where the counts come from `summary()`, `toFigureHtml()` and the inline `toHTML()` card compute topology on the mesh you hand them rather than remembering what it was, so a format artefact arrives looking like a property of your model: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} icosphereMesh(3).summary() // 642 verts, 1280 tris, extent 2.0000 …, chi=2, genus 0, watertight, area 12.5065, volume 4.1527, … stlToTriMesh(icosphereMesh(3).toStlBinary()).summary() // 3840 verts, 1280 tris, extent 2.0000 …, chi=1280, genus 0, open(1280), area 12.5065, … ``` The second line has no `volume`, because `summary()` only prints one for a watertight mesh, but `signedVolume()` on the same soup still returns 4.152741: no geometry was lost. `genus 0` is correct too, because 1280 separate triangles are 1280 discs, each of genus 0. An unexpected vertex count is usually shading rather than the file. Writing and reading are faithful, so look upstream at what shaded the mesh: | Construction | vertices | |---|---| | `boxMesh()` | 8 | | `boxMesh().shadedNormals(35.0)` | 24 | | `boxMesh().flatShaded()` | 36 | | `objToTriMesh(boxMesh().toObj())` | 8 | | `objToTriMesh(boxMesh().shadedNormals(35.0).toObj())` | 24 | `flatShaded()` un-welds every triangle, so a solid stops being watertight and its Euler characteristic becomes its triangle count. Save the *unshaded* mesh and let the renderer crease-shade it, or weld after reading. ## PLY: colours, point clouds and missing normals This example writes a four-vertex coloured square as ASCII PLY, reads it back with `PlySupport`, and converts it to a `TriMesh`. **A PLY with no normals gets `(0, 0, 1)` written for every vertex by the loader.** That is a *wrong* normal rather than a missing one, and a wrong normal shades the whole model as though it faced the camera. `toTriMesh()` drops them when the file had none, so the render bridges crease-shade for you instead. Pass `keepNormals = false` to drop them even when the file has them. - **A PLY with no `face` element is a point cloud**, and `toTriMesh()` says so rather than handing back a mesh with no triangles. Check `buffers.isPointCloud` first; for drawing those, the `plyPointCloudHere` macro renders them on the GPU as camera-facing quads. - **All-white colours are dropped.** Both bridges do this. A glTF with no `COLOR_0`, or a PLY with no `red`/`green`/`blue`, gets white written for every vertex by its loader — that carries no information and would only override the renderer's own shading with a flat white. ## Missing formats and missing features **STEP, IGES, BREP and other CAD formats** are not read. A `.step` file is NURBS surfaces trimmed against each other rather than a mesh, and Field has no CAD kernel. Export STL from FreeCAD or your CAD tool and read that. `meshFromAnyFile` on a `.step` throws rather than returning an empty mesh. **Textures and materials** do not come across into a `TriMesh`, which has positions, normals, uvs and per-vertex colours only; `assimpToTriMesh` drops the material. For a textured, rendered model use `gltfModelHere` and the [`StandardRenderer`](fabricate_renderer.md); the [Renderers](reference/renderers.md) reference page lists that path's declarations. **Point clouds** are read by `PlySupport` and drawn on the GPU by `plyPointCloudHere`, but there is no CPU point-cloud type, no surface reconstruction, and no downsampling. `convexHullMesh` over the positions and `voronoi3d` are what there is. **Gaussian splats** are better served. `SplatRaster` ([`SplatRaster.kt`](https://github.com/OpenEndedGroup/Field4/blob/main/src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/graphics/render/SplatRaster.kt)) renders a splat cloud on the CPU into PNG bytes, matching the GPU renderer's framing for the same `Config`. `SplatContactSheet` puts a whole capture in one image, and `SplatCloud` lets you crop, filter, decimate, transform and merge a cloud and write a `.compressed.ply` back out. **Animation** is not kept. `GltfSupport.MeshInstance.animationSamples` carries the node tracks Assimp reads, but `assimpToTriMesh` bakes the bind pose, and skinning is not read at all. **Stepping through a mesh pipeline** has no viewer of its own. `showMeshGrid` (several meshes side by side) and `showMeshTurntable` (one mesh from four angles) show the stages statically. **Export** is OBJ and STL only: `toObj`, `saveObj`, `toStlAscii`, `toStlBinary` and `saveStl`. Neither keeps per-vertex colours. The `.compressed.ply` writer above is for splats, not triangles. ## Fixing a mesh that looks wrong Most of these show up in `summary()`, so print it before you draw anything.
| symptom | cause | what to do | |---|---|---| | `contains no obj geometry` | the file is not what its extension says | A ZIP, a glTF or an HTML error page saved as `thing.obj`: the message says what it looks like. `meshFromAnyFile` reads most formats by their contents. | | holes, or whole faces missing | inside-out winding, open mesh | Back faces are culled exactly as a GPU culls them, so a wrongly-wound patch is not dark, it is *gone*. `fixWinding()`, then check `topology().isConsistentlyOriented`. | | looks fine, every measurement negative | inside-out winding, closed solid | The silhouette is unchanged and both renderers flip inward normals rather than shading them black, so the picture is no help at all. `signedVolume() < 0` is the only tell; `fixWinding()` is the fix. | | flat, faceted or oddly uniform shading | no normals, or invented ones | A mesh with *none* is crease-shaded for you; one with wrong ones is not. Recompute with `shadedNormals(35.0)`. To drop them, `copy(normals = null)`, or `withoutAttributes()` for every attribute. | | `isWatertight()` false on a closed solid | it came through STL | Or it was `flatShaded()` before it was written. `weld(1e-5)` recovers the topology, and `meanEdgeLength()` is the scale that tells you 1e-5 is safe rather than a guess. | | the vertex count is exactly 3× | STL, or `flatShaded()` | Both un-weld every triangle, and the reader on the other side will not weld it back. `weld`, then `shadedNormals` if you want the hard edges again. |
## From a file on disk to a solid you can cut To use a loaded mesh in a boolean, it has to be closed: [`toSolid()`](manifold.md) refuses anything that is not. Two calls do the repair automatically. `diagnose()` says what is wrong, and `repairToSolid()` fixes what it can and reports what it could not: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} val mesh = meshFromAnyFile("scan.glb") println(mesh.diagnose().report()) // why, worst first val fixed = mesh.repairToSolid() println(fixed.report()) // what was done, and what was not if (fixed.isSolid) display(fixed.mesh.toSolid() - drill) ``` ### Defect severities: what blocks a solid `diagnose()` sorts what it finds by severity. A blocking defect is one Manifold rejects; the others it accepts, though some of them still deserve a look. | defect | severity | what it means | |---|---|---| | `NON_FINITE_POSITION` | **blocking** | a `NaN` or infinite coordinate | | `UNWELDED_VERTICES` | **blocking** | coincident vertices with different indices — until they merge, every seam reads as a hole | | `DUPLICATE_FACE` | **blocking** | two triangles with the same corners; each extra copy makes its three edges non-manifold | | `NON_MANIFOLD_EDGE` | **blocking** | an edge with three or more faces | | `OPEN_BOUNDARY` | **blocking** | a hole | | `UNWALKABLE_BOUNDARY` | **blocking** | boundary edges in no closed ring | | `DEGENERATE_FACE` | suspicious | zero-area triangles — **Manifold accepts these** | | `NON_MANIFOLD_VERTEX` | suspicious | a pinch point — **Manifold accepts these** | | `INVERTED_ORIENTATION` | suspicious | closed but wound inward — **Manifold accepts this** | | `MULTIPLE_COMPONENTS` | informational | disjoint pieces — **Manifold accepts these and sums the volumes** | | `UNREFERENCED_VERTEX` | informational | vertices no triangle uses | The dangerous *suspicious* row is `INVERTED_ORIENTATION`: an inside-out closed mesh is a legal manifold, and Manifold hands back a **negative volume** without throwing, after which a boolean computes the complement of what you meant. `toSolid()` refuses it for that reason (pass `check = false` to take it anyway); `fixWinding()` flips it. `UNWALKABLE_BOUNDARY` usually means inconsistent winding rather than anything exotic. Tracing a boundary into a ring follows directed half-edges, so a wrongly wound patch breaks the trace and an ordinary hole reports as unwalkable. Run `fixWinding()` and diagnose again before reading it as two holes meeting at one vertex. ### The repair steps, in order `repairToSolid()` runs these steps in this order, because each later step gives a wrong answer without the earlier ones: | step | fixes | does **not** fix | |---|---|---| | `weld` | unwelded seams, STL-style unshared vertices | anything, until it has run: hole and component counts are meaningless before it | | `removeDegenerateTriangles` | zero-area faces | — | | `removeDuplicateFaces` | duplicated faces; a back-to-back pair cancels to nothing | — | | `removeNonManifoldFins` | dangling flaps (a non-manifold edge **and** a boundary edge on the same triangle) | two closed sheets meeting on an edge — that needs a modelling decision, so it is left alone and reported | | `fixWinding` | inconsistent orientation | — | | `fillHoles` | open boundary loops | a non-planar or self-intersecting rim gets a cap it flags as suspect | | `fixWinding` again | inside-out components | — | The second `fixWinding` does different work from the first. Its outward-facing stage only flips a component that is *closed*, because "outward" is undefined for an open sheet, so before the caps exist every holed component is skipped. Running it again afterwards is what stops a repaired mesh coming back inside out with a negative volume. **Hole filling is the part to be suspicious of.** Each ring is reversed (a cap must walk its boundary edges the opposite way to the surface), given a Newell normal, projected into that plane and ear-clipped; if ear clipping stalls, a centroid fan closes it anyway. Two failure modes are detected and reported: - **a non-planar rim** gets a flat cap over a wavy hole. The mesh is a valid solid; the *volume is wrong*. `BoundaryLoopInfo.planarity` measures the deviation against the loop's own diameter before the fill happens, so the warning is available in advance. - **a self-intersecting rim** is what makes ear clipping stall, and the fan that closes it can pass through itself. A ring that repeats a vertex is neither: it is a figure-eight, two holes pinched together, and capping it as one polygon *creates* a non-manifold edge — the repair would make the mesh worse. Those are split at the repeats first, so each real hole gets its own cap. #### A sound cap can still be the wrong shape Nothing about a hole says whether its end should be a flat cap or whether the model continued there. These two cases have equally clean caps and opposite outcomes: | Input surface | rim | cap | cap share of surface | result | |---|---|---|---|---| | uncapped cylinder | flat | clean ear clip | 16.5% | volume error **0.00000** — exactly right | | torus with its tube severed | flat | clean ear clip | 2.7% | volume error **4.2%**, and **genus 1 becomes 0** | Planarity, fill method, edge count and cap area are all as good or better on the wrong one, so no cap-area threshold could flag the torus without also flagging the cylinder. `capAreaFraction` is reported, but does not set `isSuspect`. So **`isSuspect == false` means the cap's geometry is sound, not that the model is the one you started with.** Only a comparison against the shape you meant catches the difference. ### What `repairToSolid` does Beyond what `repaired()` (weld → degenerate → unused → winding, in `mesh_topology.kt`) already does, `repairToSolid()` is responsible for exactly two families: **open boundaries**, and **non-manifold edges** from duplicated faces or dangling fins. It refuses rather than guesses on two shapes: a `NaN` position, because repairing around it would silently delete the affected triangles and cap the gap, and two closed tetrahedra sharing a face. Both report the failure instead of returning something that looks repaired. Most broken meshes repair to the shape they came from. The ones that come back valid but the wrong shape have curved or non-planar holes, where a fan fill is doing the best it can; a crowned rim can be off by a third of its volume. ??? aside "Where the repair measurements are" The table of deliberately broken meshes, what each row is broken in, and the per-row residuals are in [`dev_docs/MESH_REPAIR_MEASUREMENTS.md`](https://github.com/OpenEndedGroup/Field4/blob/main/dev_docs/MESH_REPAIR_MEASUREMENTS.md). ### Repairing ToyCar `ToyCar.glb` (77,429 vertices, 108,936 triangles, 2,197 components, 42,104 boundary edges in 2,782 traced loops) **repairs to a valid solid you can boolean**: 21,047 vertices welded, 84 holes closed with 3,668 triangles. There is no undamaged original to compare it against, so "valid solid" is all you can say about it. The volume it reports, `3.16e-5`, should not be trusted as is: nine of the 84 caps are flagged suspect, one of them a 335-edge centroid fan, a lid the size of a body panel. Look at `result.suspectFills` before trusting any measurement of a repaired model. ### Seeing it `Box.showMeshDiagnosis(mesh)` puts the mesh, painted by defect, beside the ordered list of what is wrong. `TriMesh.defectFLines()` gives the same information as drawable lines to lay over your own drawing: red for boundary loops, orange for non-manifold edges, magenta for pinched figure-eight loops, yellow (opt-in) for winding disagreements. `TriMesh.withDefectColors()` is the per-vertex colouring the card renders, if you want it in your own picture. # Geometry from disk You have a mesh file, and you want to see it in Field and then compute with it. For every format, that is one line: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} showMesh("/path/to/thing.glb") ``` That reads the file, assembles it, and puts a shaded render you can orbit into the box's output area, with the mesh's measurements printed underneath. Keep the mesh instead of the picture and everything in the [mesh family](mesh_examples.md) applies: weld it, measure its volume, decimate it, shoot a ray at it, write it back out as something else. ## What reads what
| you have | the call | what you get back | works headless | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `.obj` | `meshFromFile(path)` | `TriMesh`, index-for-index with the file | yes | | `.stl` (ASCII or binary) | `meshFromFile(path)` | `TriMesh`, triangle soup — see [below](#what-each-format-loses) | yes | | `.ply` (ASCII, binary, either endianness) | `meshFromAnyFile(path)` | `TriMesh` with the file's per-vertex colours | yes | | `.glb`, `.gltf`, `.fbx`, `.dae`, `.3ds`, … | `meshFromAnyFile(path)` | `TriMesh`, all parts baked through their node transforms | yes | | any of the above, textured, with PBR materials | `gltfModelHere("…")` / the [Fabricate renderer](fabricate_renderer.md) | GPU buffers, materials, textures, a live scene | no — needs a renderer | | `.step`, `.iges`, `.brep` | **nothing** | — | — |
`meshFromAnyFile` handles everything `meshFromFile` does and more, so if you are unsure, use it. `meshFromFile` is the pure-Kotlin reader with no native library behind it. Where each loader lives in the source is at the [end of the page](#internals-where-the-loaders-live). Two renderers put a mesh on screen, and both take a `TriMesh`. `showMesh` sends it to the Three.js viewer, where you can orbit it; it is the same viewer `threeLines(...)` draws FLines in, so a solid and its annotations can share one scene. Pass `renderer = MeshRenderer.CPU` for a still image drawn on the CPU instead, which needs no GPU; `TriMesh.renderPng` and the inline `toHTML()` card use the same renderer. ## A real GLB, in a real output area This example loads the Khronos ToyCar sample, the same GLB the [Fabricate renderer](fabricate_renderer.md) renders with full PBR materials. An artist's model is a shell rather than a solid, and every UV seam and every hard edge is a real cut in the surface. STL keeps nothing but triangles: no vertex sharing at all, so 1280 triangles become 3840 unshared vertices and every edge reads as a boundary. `weld(1e-5)` recovers the topology exactly but not the normals, because STL never stored one per vertex, so re-shade after welding — `shadedNormals(35.0)` is usually right. PLY is the format that carries colour, which is generally why a file is a PLY at all: it is what photogrammetry and scanners emit, and `meshFromAnyFile` routes `.ply` through `PlySupport` rather than Assimp for that reason. File size for the same 1280 triangles, with binary STL's exactly `84 + 50n` bytes as the floor: | Format | bytes | |---|---| | binary `.stl` | 64,084 | | `.obj` | 75,625 | | ASCII `.stl` | 324,825 | ## Where the counts come from `summary()`, `toFigureHtml()` and the inline `toHTML()` card compute topology on the mesh you hand them rather than remembering what it was, so a format artefact arrives looking like a property of your model: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} icosphereMesh(3).summary() // 642 verts, 1280 tris, extent 2.0000 …, chi=2, genus 0, watertight, area 12.5065, volume 4.1527, … stlToTriMesh(icosphereMesh(3).toStlBinary()).summary() // 3840 verts, 1280 tris, extent 2.0000 …, chi=1280, genus 0, open(1280), area 12.5065, … ``` The second line has no `volume`, because `summary()` only prints one for a watertight mesh, but `signedVolume()` on the same soup still returns 4.152741: no geometry was lost. `genus 0` is correct too, because 1280 separate triangles are 1280 discs, each of genus 0. An unexpected vertex count is usually shading rather than the file. Writing and reading are faithful, so look upstream at what shaded the mesh: | Construction | vertices | |---|---| | `boxMesh()` | 8 | | `boxMesh().shadedNormals(35.0)` | 24 | | `boxMesh().flatShaded()` | 36 | | `objToTriMesh(boxMesh().toObj())` | 8 | | `objToTriMesh(boxMesh().shadedNormals(35.0).toObj())` | 24 | `flatShaded()` un-welds every triangle, so a solid stops being watertight and its Euler characteristic becomes its triangle count. Save the *unshaded* mesh and let the renderer crease-shade it, or weld after reading. ## PLY: colours, point clouds and missing normals This example writes a four-vertex coloured square as ASCII PLY, reads it back with `PlySupport`, and converts it to a `TriMesh`. In a document of your own, `"square.ply".file` is the form to use. ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/geometry_from_disk/ply.png" wait="9.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" padding="20"} :::static // A four-vertex coloured square, written as ASCII PLY and read back. The same code path a 10-million- // point scan takes; small enough to read here. val dir = java.nio.file.Files.createTempDirectory("ply-demo").toFile() val file = java.io.File(dir, "square.ply") file.writeText( """ ply format ascii 1.0 element vertex 4 property float x property float y property float z property uchar red property uchar green property uchar blue element face 2 property list uchar int vertex_indices end_header 0 0 0 255 40 40 1 0 0 40 255 40 1 1 0 60 60 255 0 1 0 255 235 40 3 0 1 2 3 0 2 3 """.trimIndent() + "\n" ) // The loader is PlySupport — no renderer, no Vulkan, no Box context needed. val model = PlySupport.loadPly(file.path) val b = model.buffers println("vertices ${b.vertexCount}, indices ${b.indexCount}, colours ${b.hasColors}, " + "normals in the file ${b.hasNormals}, point cloud ${b.isPointCloud}") println("packed as ${b.vertexData.capacity() / (b.vertexCount * 4)} floats per vertex: " + "[pos.xyz][normal.xyz][color.rgba]") // ...and the bridge into a TriMesh keeps the colours. val mesh = model.toTriMesh() println("as a TriMesh: ${mesh.summary()}") println("colours survived: ${mesh.hasColors}, vertex 0 is ${mesh.color(0)}") println("normals dropped: ${!mesh.hasNormals} — the file had none, and the loader's " + "invented (0,0,1) would shade the whole thing as if it faced you") :::fold draw it flat on, then clean up showMesh( mesh, view = MeshView(yawDegrees = 0.0, pitchDegrees = 0.0, width = 420, height = 315), title = "square.ply — per-vertex colours", ) dir.deleteRecursively() :::endfold ``` ![A two-triangle square rendered flat on, its four corners coloured red, green, blue and yellow with the colours interpolating smoothly across each triangle and meeting along the shared diagonal, captioned 4 verts, 2 tris, extent 1.000 x 1.000 x 0.000, chi=1, open](assets/geometry_from_disk/ply.png) Three details in that output are easy to miss: - **A PLY with no normals gets `(0, 0, 1)` written for every vertex by the loader.** That is a *wrong* normal rather than a missing one, and a wrong normal shades the whole model as though it faced the camera. `toTriMesh()` drops them when the file had none, so the render bridges crease-shade for you instead. Pass `keepNormals = false` to drop them even when the file has them. - **A PLY with no `face` element is a point cloud**, and `toTriMesh()` says so rather than handing back a mesh with no triangles. Check `buffers.isPointCloud` first; for drawing those, the `plyPointCloudHere` macro renders them on the GPU as camera-facing quads. - **All-white colours are dropped.** Both bridges do this. A glTF with no `COLOR_0`, or a PLY with no `red`/`green`/`blue`, gets white written for every vertex by its loader — that carries no information and would only override the renderer's own shading with a flat white. ## Missing formats and missing features **STEP, IGES, BREP and other CAD formats** are not read. A `.step` file is NURBS surfaces trimmed against each other rather than a mesh, and Field has no CAD kernel. Export STL from FreeCAD or your CAD tool and read that. `meshFromAnyFile` on a `.step` throws rather than returning an empty mesh. **Textures and materials** do not come across into a `TriMesh`, which has positions, normals, uvs and per-vertex colours only; `assimpToTriMesh` drops the material. For a textured, rendered model use `gltfModelHere` and the [`StandardRenderer`](fabricate_renderer.md); the [Renderers](reference/renderers.md) reference page lists that path's declarations. **Point clouds** are read by `PlySupport` and drawn on the GPU by `plyPointCloudHere`, but there is no CPU point-cloud type, no surface reconstruction, and no downsampling. `convexHullMesh` over the positions and `voronoi3d` are what there is. **Gaussian splats** are better served. `SplatRaster` ([`SplatRaster.kt`](https://github.com/OpenEndedGroup/Field4/blob/main/src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/graphics/render/SplatRaster.kt)) renders a splat cloud on the CPU into PNG bytes, matching the GPU renderer's framing for the same `Config`. `SplatContactSheet` puts a whole capture in one image, and `SplatCloud` lets you crop, filter, decimate, transform and merge a cloud and write a `.compressed.ply` back out. **Animation** is not kept. `GltfSupport.MeshInstance.animationSamples` carries the node tracks Assimp reads, but `assimpToTriMesh` bakes the bind pose, and skinning is not read at all. **Stepping through a mesh pipeline** has no viewer of its own. `showMeshGrid` (several meshes side by side) and `showMeshTurntable` (one mesh from four angles) show the stages statically. **Export** is OBJ and STL only: `toObj`, `saveObj`, `toStlAscii`, `toStlBinary` and `saveStl`. Neither keeps per-vertex colours. The `.compressed.ply` writer above is for splats, not triangles. ## Fixing a mesh that looks wrong Most of these show up in `summary()`, so print it before you draw anything.
| symptom | cause | what to do | |---|---|---| | `contains no obj geometry` | the file is not what its extension says | A ZIP, a glTF or an HTML error page saved as `thing.obj`: the message says what it looks like. `meshFromAnyFile` reads most formats by their contents. | | holes, or whole faces missing | inside-out winding, open mesh | Back faces are culled exactly as a GPU culls them, so a wrongly-wound patch is not dark, it is *gone*. `fixWinding()`, then check `topology().isConsistentlyOriented`. | | looks fine, every measurement negative | inside-out winding, closed solid | The silhouette is unchanged and both renderers flip inward normals rather than shading them black, so the picture is no help at all. `signedVolume() < 0` is the only tell; `fixWinding()` is the fix. | | flat, faceted or oddly uniform shading | no normals, or invented ones | A mesh with *none* is crease-shaded for you; one with wrong ones is not. Recompute with `shadedNormals(35.0)`. To drop them, `copy(normals = null)`, or `withoutAttributes()` for every attribute. | | `isWatertight()` false on a closed solid | it came through STL | Or it was `flatShaded()` before it was written. `weld(1e-5)` recovers the topology, and `meanEdgeLength()` is the scale that tells you 1e-5 is safe rather than a guess. | | the vertex count is exactly 3× | STL, or `flatShaded()` | Both un-weld every triangle, and the reader on the other side will not weld it back. `weld`, then `shadedNormals` if you want the hard edges again. |
## From a file on disk to a solid you can cut To use a loaded mesh in a boolean, it has to be closed: [`toSolid()`](manifold.md) refuses anything that is not. Two calls do the repair automatically. `diagnose()` says what is wrong, and `repairToSolid()` fixes what it can and reports what it could not: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} val mesh = meshFromAnyFile("scan.glb") println(mesh.diagnose().report()) // why, worst first val fixed = mesh.repairToSolid() println(fixed.report()) // what was done, and what was not if (fixed.isSolid) display(fixed.mesh.toSolid() - drill) ``` ### Defect severities: what blocks a solid `diagnose()` sorts what it finds by severity. A blocking defect is one Manifold rejects; the others it accepts, though some of them still deserve a look. | defect | severity | what it means | |---|---|---| | `NON_FINITE_POSITION` | **blocking** | a `NaN` or infinite coordinate | | `UNWELDED_VERTICES` | **blocking** | coincident vertices with different indices — until they merge, every seam reads as a hole | | `DUPLICATE_FACE` | **blocking** | two triangles with the same corners; each extra copy makes its three edges non-manifold | | `NON_MANIFOLD_EDGE` | **blocking** | an edge with three or more faces | | `OPEN_BOUNDARY` | **blocking** | a hole | | `UNWALKABLE_BOUNDARY` | **blocking** | boundary edges in no closed ring | | `DEGENERATE_FACE` | suspicious | zero-area triangles — **Manifold accepts these** | | `NON_MANIFOLD_VERTEX` | suspicious | a pinch point — **Manifold accepts these** | | `INVERTED_ORIENTATION` | suspicious | closed but wound inward — **Manifold accepts this** | | `MULTIPLE_COMPONENTS` | informational | disjoint pieces — **Manifold accepts these and sums the volumes** | | `UNREFERENCED_VERTEX` | informational | vertices no triangle uses | The dangerous *suspicious* row is `INVERTED_ORIENTATION`: an inside-out closed mesh is a legal manifold, and Manifold hands back a **negative volume** without throwing, after which a boolean computes the complement of what you meant. `toSolid()` refuses it for that reason (pass `check = false` to take it anyway); `fixWinding()` flips it. `UNWALKABLE_BOUNDARY` usually means inconsistent winding rather than anything exotic. Tracing a boundary into a ring follows directed half-edges, so a wrongly wound patch breaks the trace and an ordinary hole reports as unwalkable. Run `fixWinding()` and diagnose again before reading it as two holes meeting at one vertex. ### The repair steps, in order `repairToSolid()` runs these steps in this order, because each later step gives a wrong answer without the earlier ones: | step | fixes | does **not** fix | |---|---|---| | `weld` | unwelded seams, STL-style unshared vertices | anything, until it has run: hole and component counts are meaningless before it | | `removeDegenerateTriangles` | zero-area faces | — | | `removeDuplicateFaces` | duplicated faces; a back-to-back pair cancels to nothing | — | | `removeNonManifoldFins` | dangling flaps (a non-manifold edge **and** a boundary edge on the same triangle) | two closed sheets meeting on an edge — that needs a modelling decision, so it is left alone and reported | | `fixWinding` | inconsistent orientation | — | | `fillHoles` | open boundary loops | a non-planar or self-intersecting rim gets a cap it flags as suspect | | `fixWinding` again | inside-out components | — | The second `fixWinding` does different work from the first. Its outward-facing stage only flips a component that is *closed*, because "outward" is undefined for an open sheet, so before the caps exist every holed component is skipped. Running it again afterwards is what stops a repaired mesh coming back inside out with a negative volume. **Hole filling is the part to be suspicious of.** Each ring is reversed (a cap must walk its boundary edges the opposite way to the surface), given a Newell normal, projected into that plane and ear-clipped; if ear clipping stalls, a centroid fan closes it anyway. Two failure modes are detected and reported: - **a non-planar rim** gets a flat cap over a wavy hole. The mesh is a valid solid; the *volume is wrong*. `BoundaryLoopInfo.planarity` measures the deviation against the loop's own diameter before the fill happens, so the warning is available in advance. - **a self-intersecting rim** is what makes ear clipping stall, and the fan that closes it can pass through itself. A ring that repeats a vertex is neither: it is a figure-eight, two holes pinched together, and capping it as one polygon *creates* a non-manifold edge — the repair would make the mesh worse. Those are split at the repeats first, so each real hole gets its own cap. #### A sound cap can still be the wrong shape Nothing about a hole says whether its end should be a flat cap or whether the model continued there. These two cases have equally clean caps and opposite outcomes: | Input surface | rim | cap | cap share of surface | result | |---|---|---|---|---| | uncapped cylinder | flat | clean ear clip | 16.5% | volume error **0.00000** — exactly right | | torus with its tube severed | flat | clean ear clip | 2.7% | volume error **4.2%**, and **genus 1 becomes 0** | Planarity, fill method, edge count and cap area are all as good or better on the wrong one, so no cap-area threshold could flag the torus without also flagging the cylinder. `capAreaFraction` is reported, but does not set `isSuspect`. So **`isSuspect == false` means the cap's geometry is sound, not that the model is the one you started with.** Only a comparison against the shape you meant catches the difference. ### What `repairToSolid` does Beyond what `repaired()` (weld → degenerate → unused → winding, in `mesh_topology.kt`) already does, `repairToSolid()` is responsible for exactly two families: **open boundaries**, and **non-manifold edges** from duplicated faces or dangling fins. It refuses rather than guesses on two shapes: a `NaN` position, because repairing around it would silently delete the affected triangles and cap the gap, and two closed tetrahedra sharing a face. Both report the failure instead of returning something that looks repaired. Most broken meshes repair to the shape they came from. The ones that come back valid but the wrong shape have curved or non-planar holes, where a fan fill is doing the best it can; a crowned rim can be off by a third of its volume. ??? aside "Where the repair measurements are" The table of deliberately broken meshes, what each row is broken in, and the per-row residuals are in [`dev_docs/MESH_REPAIR_MEASUREMENTS.md`](https://github.com/OpenEndedGroup/Field4/blob/main/dev_docs/MESH_REPAIR_MEASUREMENTS.md). ### Repairing ToyCar `ToyCar.glb` (77,429 vertices, 108,936 triangles, 2,197 components, 42,104 boundary edges in 2,782 traced loops) **repairs to a valid solid you can boolean**: 21,047 vertices welded, 84 holes closed with 3,668 triangles. There are three calls for turning it into coordinates, and they promise different things: | verb | what you give it | what it promises | |---|---|---| | `realize(policy)` | a topology, with or without coordinates | coordinates built from the combinatorics by a declared construction | | `relax(plan)` | an embedding you already have | that embedding, improved under a declared set of named constraints | | `canonicalize(...)` | an embedding, or none | the symmetric representative, with stated guarantees, and a reported failure when they do not apply | The realization policies each operator uses by default (centroid dual, edge-midpoint ambo, face-normal kis, along-edge truncation, gyro subdivision) are local rules of thumb. In the `gyro` figure the new faces stay flat on the squares they subdivided: the combinatorics of `gC` are those of the pentagonal icositetrahedron, but its coordinates are not. ### `relax(...)`: repair the embedding you have `relax(plan)` runs a pure-Kotlin nonlinear least-squares pass over the vertex coordinates. A `RelaxationPlan` is a list of named, immutable constraint values (`edge-length`, `face-planarity`, `centroid`, `common-radius`, `proximity`, `edge-tangency`, `tangency-centroid`, `symmetry-orbit`) plus a least-squares configuration and an optional gauge. Because the plan is a value you can print, compare and reweight (`plan.withWeight("edge-length", 0.0)`), and the result reports each family's error before and after, you can see which constraint gave way. Topology and attributes are unchanged; only the coordinates are replaced. The figure below calls `solveRealization()`, a shorthand that turns five weights into `RelaxationPlan.regularize()`. !!! warning "`relax` is a local least-squares pass" Levenberg–Marquardt from the supplied embedding is a **local** method, and the `referenceWeight` term biases it toward where it started, so what you get is a general constraint relaxation and not the unique Conway canonical form. Nothing here checks for self-intersection or inversion, and degenerate faces are *reported* rather than repaired. The defaults suit the symmetric finite polyhedra this page produces. For a shape that is meant to be irregular, turn the common-radius and edge-tangency families off. Pass a target if you want a particular size. ### `canonicalize(...)`: the form the combinatorics already determined The canonical form of a polyhedron is the embedding where every edge is tangent to one common sphere, the centroid of those tangency points is the origin, and every face is planar. For the polyhedra this library produces, it is unique: !!! info "When the canonical form is unique" For a convex polyhedron (by Steinitz's theorem, for any 3-connected planar graph) the canonical form **exists and is unique** up to Möbius transformations of the sphere. Pinning the tangency centroid at the origin picks one representative; the gauge removes the remaining rigid and scale freedom. That covers every Conway operator over a Platonic seed, which is to say everything on this page. Nothing is guaranteed for non-convex, self-intersecting, higher-genus or non-3-connected input. There, the run still returns `converged` and its diagnostics, and expects you to look. There are two methods. `RECIPROCAL` is Hart's dual reciprocation, which converges in tens of iterations. `LOCAL_RELAXATION` alternates planarizing, tangentifying and recentring, and takes thousands of small steps. The default runs the first and polishes with the second. There are three calls for turning it into coordinates, and they promise different things: | verb | what you give it | what it promises | |---|---|---| | `realize(policy)` | a topology, with or without coordinates | coordinates built from the combinatorics by a declared construction | | `relax(plan)` | an embedding you already have | that embedding, improved under a declared set of named constraints | | `canonicalize(...)` | an embedding, or none | the symmetric representative, with stated guarantees, and a reported failure when they do not apply | The realization policies each operator uses by default (centroid dual, edge-midpoint ambo, face-normal kis, along-edge truncation, gyro subdivision) are local rules of thumb. In the `gyro` figure the new faces stay flat on the squares they subdivided: the combinatorics of `gC` are those of the pentagonal icositetrahedron, but its coordinates are not. ### `relax(...)`: repair the embedding you have `relax(plan)` runs a pure-Kotlin nonlinear least-squares pass over the vertex coordinates. A `RelaxationPlan` is a list of named, immutable constraint values (`edge-length`, `face-planarity`, `centroid`, `common-radius`, `proximity`, `edge-tangency`, `tangency-centroid`, `symmetry-orbit`) plus a least-squares configuration and an optional gauge. Because the plan is a value you can print, compare and reweight (`plan.withWeight("edge-length", 0.0)`), and the result reports each family's error before and after, you can see which constraint gave way. Topology and attributes are unchanged; only the coordinates are replaced. The figure below calls `solveRealization()`, a shorthand that turns five weights into `RelaxationPlan.regularize()`. !!! warning "`relax` is a local least-squares pass" Levenberg–Marquardt from the supplied embedding is a **local** method, and the `referenceWeight` term biases it toward where it started, so what you get is a general constraint relaxation and not the unique Conway canonical form. Nothing here checks for self-intersection or inversion, and degenerate faces are *reported* rather than repaired. The defaults suit the symmetric finite polyhedra this page produces. For a shape that is meant to be irregular, turn the common-radius and edge-tangency families off. For the canonical form, ask for it by name: that is the next section. ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/polytope_examples/realization.png" wait="3.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="1220" h="780" padding="14"} :::static import kotlin.random.Random // Take a real Conway output and jitter every vertex. Pass a target if you want a particular size. ### `canonicalize(...)`: the form the combinatorics already determined The canonical form of a polyhedron is the embedding where every edge is tangent to one common sphere, the centroid of those tangency points is the origin, and every face is planar. For the polyhedra this library produces, it is unique: !!! info "When the canonical form is unique" For a convex polyhedron (by Steinitz's theorem, for any 3-connected planar graph) the canonical form **exists and is unique** up to Möbius transformations of the sphere. Pinning the tangency centroid at the origin picks one representative; the gauge removes the remaining rigid and scale freedom. That covers every Conway operator over a Platonic seed, which is to say everything on this page. Nothing is guaranteed for non-convex, self-intersecting, higher-genus or non-3-connected input. There, the run still returns `converged` and its diagnostics, and expects you to look. There are two methods. `RECIPROCAL` is Hart's dual reciprocation, which converges in tens of iterations. `LOCAL_RELAXATION` alternates planarizing, tangentifying and recentring, and takes thousands of small steps. The default runs the first and polishes with the second. Each cell counts the seeds that found an exactly correct circuit: five seeds per cell, three for the
last two rows.

| problem | widths | budget | random (control) | hill climb | evolution |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

a bit-error rate of 0.125: that is `sum = Xor3(a, b, c)` with `c_out = And(a, b)`, right on six of

evolution (3/5 each) and hill climbing finds nothing at all: it converges on a two-gate design
that is 3% wrong and cannot get off it. Those spaces are small enough that sampling them is a
perfectly good algorithm.

**Or-reduce cannot be done without recursion**, which is what makes it the positive result.
Morpho sizes a LUT cell to its widest operand and broadcasts the narrow ones (`compiler.js:964#const w = Math.max(...inputs.map(x => x.length));`):

### Why the width family is 2, 3 and 5

Selecting on widths 2, 4 and 8 produced **400 distinct correct `or-reduce` designs**. Re-compiled at
twelve other widths, all 400 are correct at 3, 6, 12, 16, 32 and 48; **399 of them are wrong at
5, 7 and 9**. Exactly one design in four hundred is actually parametric. The dual, `and-reduce`,
gives **zero of 400**.

The mechanism is a hole in the language, not a quirk of the search. `SPLIT` halves a bus as
`floor(w/2), w - floor(w/2)` (`primitives.js:42#const half = Math.floor(w.length / 2);`), so the two halves are the same width exactly when
the width is even; 5, 7 and 9 are the small widths where they differ *and* both are wider than one
bit. A LUT applied to both halves (`Or(x0, x1)`, which is what these designs do) then has operands
of two different widths, and `materializeLut` (`compiler.js:962-973`) takes the maximum and
broadcasts only operands of width **1**. Unequal wider operands are neither broadcast nor rejected:
the extra pins simply read past the end of the shorter bus. The circuit is silently wrong, and a search that has never been shown an odd width has
no way to find out.

Change the family to 2, 3 and 5 (one line) and **400 of 400 designs are correct at every width
tried**, from 2 to 48. That family is `MorphoProblems.ODD_FAMILY`, the default for the reduction
problems, and `a power of two width family selects designs that are not parametric` is the test that
holds the claim in place.

A parametric design is a claim about all N, and one width is one point: that on its own is the case
for scoring at several widths. What several widths also catch is undefined behaviour in the
compiler, exploited by a search that had no idea it was cheating.

### The recursive adder

Nothing finds a divide-and-conquer adder. Not random sampling, not hill climbing, not a population,
not with lexicase selection over per-bit test cases, not with a width curriculum, and not with both
`SPLIT`s handed over as an unremovable prologue.

The near miss is not uniform across the drivers, and the difference is informative. Random sampling
and hill climbing stop on **depth-1** circuits: broadcast logic, no recursion at all, bit-error rates
around 0.25 to 0.27. Evolution at 20 000 invocations gets to **16 gates and depth 8**, which is
`ripple_adder`'s cost profile exactly, and is still **17.9% wrong**. It has found the shape and not
the wiring: eight levels of something chained across the width, carrying the wrong thing.

Three measurements say why the rest of the way is so far.

*The target is in the space.* The ripple skeleton, written by hand in the generator's own grammar,
is five statements and scores exactly `ripple_adder`: 16 gates and depth 8 at eight bits, 64 gates
and depth 32 at thirty-two. `the recursive adder is reachable in the genome grammar` asserts it.

*The recursion is being tried and is not paying.* Of 4 000 random programs on the guided problem,
511 (12.8%) contain a self-call in the compiled circuit. The best of those scores 0.2880 and the
best purely combinational candidate scores 0.3017. An eighth of the population is recursing, for
1.4% of the error. On the unguided problem only 2.8% recurse, and the best of those is *worse* than
the best combinational one (0.3753 against 0.3017); the two `SPLIT`s are the difference.
(`MorphoSearchMeasurements.recursionDensity`.)

*And the reason is arithmetic about the answer.* A correct adder needs both halves recursed, both
carries chained in the right order, and the two sums `CAT`ed back: four statements worth nothing
until all four are right and wired to the outputs. Or-reduce needs two, and half of it already pays.

### Why the width family is 2, 3 and 5

Selecting on widths 2, 4 and 8 produced **400 distinct correct `or-reduce` designs**. Re-compiled at
twelve other widths, all 400 are correct at 3, 6, 12, 16, 32 and 48; **399 of them are wrong at
5, 7 and 9**. Exactly one design in four hundred is actually parametric. The dual, `and-reduce`,
gives **zero of 400**.

The mechanism is a hole in the language, not a quirk of the search. `SPLIT` halves a bus as
`floor(w/2), w - floor(w/2)` (`primitives.js:42#const half = Math.floor(w.length / 2);`), so the two halves are the same width exactly when
the width is even; 5, 7 and 9 are the small widths where they differ *and* both are wider than one
bit. A LUT applied to both halves (`Or(x0, x1)`, which is what these designs do) then has operands
of two different widths, and `materializeLut` (`compiler.js:962-973`) takes the maximum and
broadcasts only operands of width **1**. Unequal wider operands are neither broadcast nor rejected:
the extra pins simply read past the end of the shorter bus. The circuit is silently wrong, and a search that has never been shown an odd width has
no way to find out.

Change the family to 2, 3 and 5 (one line) and **400 of 400 designs are correct at every width
tried**, from 2 to 48. That family is `MorphoProblems.ODD_FAMILY`, the default for the reduction
problems, and `a power of two width family selects designs that are not parametric` is the test that
holds the claim in place.

A parametric design is a claim about all N, and one width is one point: that on its own is the case
for scoring at several widths. What several widths also catch is undefined behaviour in the
compiler, exploited by a search that had no idea it was cheating.

### The recursive adder

Nothing finds a divide-and-conquer adder. Not random sampling, not hill climbing, not a population,
not with lexicase selection over per-bit test cases, not with a width curriculum, and not with both
`SPLIT`s handed over as an unremovable prologue.

The near miss is not uniform across the drivers, and the difference is informative. Random sampling
and hill climbing stop on **depth-1** circuits: broadcast logic, no recursion at all, bit-error rates
around 0.25 to 0.27. Evolution at 20 000 invocations gets to **16 gates and depth 8**, which is
`ripple_adder`'s cost profile exactly, and is still **17.9% wrong**. It has found the shape and not
the wiring: eight levels of something chained across the width, carrying the wrong thing.

Three measurements say why the rest of the way is so far.

*The target is in the space.* The ripple skeleton, written by hand in the generator's own grammar,
is five statements and scores exactly `ripple_adder`: 16 gates and depth 8 at eight bits, 64 gates
and depth 32 at thirty-two. `the recursive adder is reachable in the genome grammar` asserts it.

*The recursion is being tried and is not paying.* Of 4 000 random programs on the guided problem,
511 (12.8%) contain a self-call in the compiled circuit. The best of those scores 0.2880 and the
best purely combinational candidate scores 0.3017. An eighth of the population is recursing, for
1.4% of the error. On the unguided problem only 2.8% recurse, and the best of those is *worse* than
the best combinational one (0.3753 against 0.3017); the two `SPLIT`s are the difference.
(`MorphoSearchMeasurements.recursionDensity`.)

*And the reason is arithmetic about the answer.* A correct adder needs both halves recursed, both
carries chained in the right order, and the two sums `CAT`ed back: four statements worth nothing
until all four are right and wired to the outputs. Or-reduce needs two, and half of it already pays.
